analysis.one_liner: Requires asbestos bankruptcy trusts to publicly report each claimant's name, exposure history, and payments.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a vote, having drawn only one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company facing asbestos lawsuits goes bankrupt, a court-supervised trust takes over and pays the victims. This bill would require every such trust to file quarterly public reports naming each claimant, describing their exposure history, and explaining each payment. Supporters called it a fraud deterrent; critics said it hands detailed claimant data to the corporations still fighting asbestos victims in court. The bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee in May 2014 and never received any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that face asbestos liability lawsuits. The quarterly reports and on-request disclosures would give their lawyers a detailed, public record of every trust claimant's name, exposure history, and payment basis — information they could use to challenge claims and to cross-examine plaintiffs in court. Defense-side organizations that backed the bill described this as transparency aimed at fraud; the data flows one way, from victims to defendants.

how_it_helps.text: Each asbestos bankruptcy trust would have to file quarterly reports on the court's public docket describing every demand it received, including the claimant's name and exposure history, and the basis for any payment.
The reports would exclude confidential medical records and the claimant's full Social Security number, which supporters cited as protecting victims' most sensitive information.
Trusts would have to provide, on written request and possibly for a fee, any information about payments and demands to any party to a lawsuit involving asbestos liability.
Supporters' stated purpose was public transparency about trust payouts as a check on fraudulent or duplicate claims.

analysis.who_pays: People with asbestos-related disease — mostly older workers, veterans, and their families — who filed or will file claims. Their names, exposure histories, and payment details would become public and available to defendant companies. Trusts would also bear the cost of producing the reports and responding to requests, which the trusts could pass on to claimants through the fees the bill lets them charge.

drawbacks.text: The bill is one-sided: it compels detailed disclosure only from the trusts that pay victims, not from the defendant companies and their insurers who would receive the data, so it functions mainly as a litigation tool for one side.

Even with medical records and full Social Security numbers excluded, publishing each claimant's name and exposure history on a public docket exposes private facts about seriously ill people and their families.
New reporting requirements and per-request fees could slow trust payments to terminally ill claimants, for whom delays have real consequences.
Supporters presented no evidence in the bill or its summary of widespread fraud at asbestos trusts; the measure imposes new burdens on all claimants regardless.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated goal — public accountability for trusts that pay out billions — has some legitimacy, but the bill's design undercuts it. It demands granular disclosure from only one side of asbestos litigation, hands that disclosure to the companies still suing victims, and offers victims no comparable transparency about their opponents. For the people the trusts exist to compensate, the likely effects are lost privacy and slower payments.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Flake introduced the bill on May 12, 2014, with one Republican cosponsor.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Asbestos victims and their families, whose claim details stayed private and whose trust payments faced no new delays, and the trusts, which avoided a new reporting burden. The corporate defendants who would have gained the claimant data got nothing, because the bill never moved.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only cosponsor.

for.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and defense-side business groups
for.what_they_did: Publicly championed the FACT Act across multiple Congresses as a transparency measure against asbestos claim fraud.

against.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or committee vote; it sat in committee until Congress ended.

against.name: Asbestos victims' advocacy groups and plaintiffs' attorneys
against.what_they_did: Opposed the FACT Act across multiple Congresses, arguing it strips victims' privacy and arms defendants with data to delay or deny payments.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred. All recorded sponsorship was Republican — Flake plus one Republican cosponsor — and the committee chairman who declined to act was a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill would hand these companies a public, searchable record of every trust claimant's name, exposure history, and payment basis to use against them in court. Their gain is the victims' loss of privacy and leverage.

Trusts exist to compensate victims after the liable company goes bankrupt; the bill adds quarterly reporting duties and per-request production costs they would have to absorb, likely at claimants' expense.
